---
title: "Releases, revisions and comparability"
description: "How to compare BNR statistics across releases and periods."
---

BNR identifies public releases so that users can tell which data and methods produced a result. Figures may be revised when source information improves or a controlled correction is required.

## Why this matters

A value copied from an earlier briefing may not be identical to a later dashboard value for the same period. The difference may reflect later records, resolved outcomes, source corrections or a defined method change.

## Types of change

| Change | Example | Effect on comparison |
|---|---|---|
| **Data maturation** | A late record or completed outcome is added | Recent values may change |
| **Correction** | A duplicate or invalid date is resolved | A previous value is replaced through a controlled release |
| **Method revision** | A denominator source or classification rule changes | The series may require a documented break or recalculation |
| **Presentation change** | Labels or layout improve without changing values | Statistical comparability is unchanged |

## Stable and release-stamped outputs

A stable “current” file is convenient for users who need the latest approved data. A release-stamped file supports reproducibility because it identifies the exact historical release used in an analysis.

For research or formal reporting, retain the release identifier, coverage date, dataset metadata and access date rather than relying only on a copied value.

## Release date and data period

The **release date** is the date on which an approved package is published. The **latest data period** is the most recent observation represented in that package. They are not necessarily the same.

This distinction is especially visible in mortality surveillance, where death-certificate processing and classification may mean that the latest complete calendar period predates the publication date. A release published in 2026 can therefore legitimately contain data ending in 2025 or earlier.

Always use the displayed coverage period when describing how current the underlying data are.

## Comparing periods

Before interpreting a change, check:

1. the event or measure definition;
2. source coverage;
3. population denominator and age standard;
4. completeness and reporting delay;
5. stratification and suppression; and
6. whether the series was revised.

::: {.callout-warning title="A break in method can resemble a change in health"}
When a data source, definition or coverage rule changes, part of the apparent trend may be methodological. BNR will identify material breaks rather than silently combining incompatible series.
:::

## What to remember

- Use release-stamped products when reproducibility matters.
- Revisions should be traceable and explained.
- Compare compatible definitions and sources.
- A revised value should replace, not silently coexist with, the superseded current value.
